tour.title: Chinatown, Little India & Kampong Glam
tour.summary: A temple, a hawker centre, a rainbow villa and a golden-domed mosque — three immigrant districts, one long MRT hop, and the story of how a colonial filing system became a nation's heritage.
tour.overviewText:
Minutes apart by MRT sit three of the most distinct neighbourhoods you will ever walk through, and this route links them: Chinatown, Little India and Kampong Glam. To understand why they exist at all you have to go back to 1819, when the British East India Company set up a trading post on this island, and then to 1822, when Stamford Raffles — the company man who founded the settlement — drew up a town plan that sorted the population by ethnicity.

That plan, drawn by Lieutenant Philip Jackson and remembered as the Raffles Town Plan, put European traders and government in one quarter, Chinese migrants south-west of the Singapore River, Indians further up the river, and Malays, Arabs and Bugis in Kampong Glam around the Sultan's palace. It was a colonial filing system, and it was never airtight: mosques were built inside the Chinese zone, the island's first Hindu temple stands on Chinatown's main street, and Chinese shopkeepers traded in Little India. What began as segregation hardened over a century into the districts you are about to walk, and in the 1980s the state changed its mind about them — demolishing shophouse quarters elsewhere while conserving these three as heritage. The shophouse is the city's vernacular building: a shop below, a home above, and a covered arcade called the five-foot way running along the front to shade the street.

Singapore still runs on an ethnic framework, the CMIO model — Chinese, Malay, Indian, Other — that shapes language policy, public housing and even elections. The Housing and Development Board's Ethnic Integration Policy of 1989 caps how many households of each group may live in a public-housing block, so that whole estates cannot quietly resegregate. Supporters say it forces daily mixing and keeps the peace; critics say the categories are blunt and the quotas can trap sellers. You do not have to settle the argument to walk through it — you will simply see the result: a Chinese temple, a Hindu temple and a mosque within a few hundred metres of one another, and a hawker centre where everyone queues at the same stalls. That open-air cooked-food centre, the hawker centre, went onto UNESCO's intangible-heritage list in 2020 as a set of "community dining rooms".

The walk starts in Chinatown and moves north through Little India to Kampong Glam, with one long MRT hop across the only real gap; end to end the route measures about 5.7 km on foot, but 3.4 km of that is the stretch between Chinatown and Little India, which you ride, leaving barely two and a half kilometres of actual walking. Do it in the morning, before the heat peaks. Singapore dollars (S$) are the currency; tap a contactless bank card or a SimplyGo card on the MRT. The temples are free but ask for covered shoulders and knees and shoes off at the door; the mosque keeps short visiting hours and closes to visitors on Fridays. May is hot and humid, so carry water. Take your time — the point of this walk is not the buildings, it is how a city of migrants learned to live beside itself.
tour.difficulty: Easy walking, hard climate. The ground is flat and paved throughout, but the heat is the real obstacle; the long leg between Chinatown and Little India is ridden by MRT, not walked, and the rest is short and level. Temples require shoes off and some have steps and thresholds. Plan a rest and a drink at each hawker stop.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 8 to 9am so you reach Chinatown's temples and the hawker centre before the worst heat and the lunch crush, and finish in Kampong Glam in the late afternoon or early evening when Haji Lane wakes up. Avoid Fridays for the mosque, which closes to visitors that day, and note the Hindu temples shut through the middle of the day.

stops.name: Sri Mariamman Temple
stops.narration:
Look up before you go in. That tower over the gate is a gopuram, the entrance pyramid of a South Indian temple, and this one rises in six tiers of painted plaster gods, each tier slightly smaller than the one below so the whole thing seems taller than it is. The present six-storey tower went up in 1925; the first, a slimmer three-tier version, dates from 1903. The two figures flanking the doorway are Murugan on the right and Krishna on the left.

This is the oldest Hindu temple in Singapore, founded in 1827 by Naraina Pillai, a Tamil clerk from Penang who had arrived with Raffles on the founder's second visit in 1819. The oldest brick parts of what you see date to 1843, and the temple has been repaired and reconsecrated many times since; its most recent reconsecration, a ritual called kumbhabhishekham that renews the gods' power, was in 2023. For most of the nineteenth century this was more than a place of worship: it sheltered newly arrived Indian immigrants until they found work and lodging, and for years its priest was the only person authorised to solemnise Hindu marriages in the colony.

The goddess is Mariamman, a rural mother goddess from South India, worshipped above all for protection against disease — in the days when smallpox and fevers swept crowded quarters, a village would build her a shrine and pray. Find the second most important shrine in the compound, that of Draupadi, a heroine of the Mahabharata epic. She matters because of the fire-walking festival, thimithi, held here about a week before Deepavali, the Hindu festival of lights. Devotees prepare for weeks, then walk barefoot across a bed of burning coals to fulfil a vow; the procession to the temple sets out from Little India, where you are headed later. If you are here in October or November, ask at the gate whether it falls during your visit.

This is a working temple, not a museum. Shoes off at the entrance, walk clockwise around the shrines, keep your voice down and never point a lens at someone praying. Entry is free; a small permit is charged if you want to take photographs seriously, and donations are welcome. Hours run in two sessions, roughly early morning to midday and again in the evening, with the temple closed through the hottest hours — confirm at the gate, because prayer times shift.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry; donations are welcome, and a small photography permit is charged (a few S$) if you want to take pictures properly. Verify the current permit price at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily in two sessions, roughly 6:00–12:00 and 18:00–21:00 (Fridays until about 21:15), and closed through the middle of the day. Prayer times shift with the calendar — confirm at the gate.
stops.accessibility: Level entry from the pavement, then a step or two into the halls. Shoes come off, so the floors are smooth and cool underfoot. Can be very crowded at festival times.
stops.insiderTip: Count the tiers of the gopuram and watch each one shrink as it rises — that is deliberate, an illusion of height. Inside, look for the Draupadi shrine, and ask about thimithi if you are travelling in October or November.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the temple and walk north along South Bridge Road for about a hundred and twenty metres, keeping the gopuram behind you. The big red-and-gold temple on the same side, with the tall shophouses around it, is the Buddha Tooth Relic Temple.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Buddha Tooth Relic Temple
stops.narration:
The temple in front of you is barely old enough to vote, and it is already one of the busiest Buddhist sites in the country. It opened on Vesak Day in 2007 — Vesak being the festival that marks the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death — and it was built by the Chinese Buddhist community around a single claim: that it holds a tooth of the historical Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama. The tooth, the story goes, was found in a collapsed stupa, a burial mound reliquary, in Myanmar. It measures about seven and a half centimetres, which is far too long to be a human tooth, so whether it is genuine is a matter of faith rather than anatomy. Say that plainly: this is a relic of devotion, not a forensic exhibit.

The architecture makes a deliberate point. Most old Chinese temples in Chinatown are southern Chinese, all curving swallowtail roofs and crowded ornament. This one is built in the style of the Tang dynasty, the golden age of Chinese art a thousand years earlier — grand, red-lacquered and symmetrical. Walk in through the heavy studded doors of the mountain gate and you are in the Hundred Dragon Hall, where a fifteen-foot Buddha Maitreya sits enthroned, Maitreya being the future Buddha who is yet to come. Behind and above are halls for Guanyin, the bodhisattva — an enlightened being who stays behind to help others — of compassion, and a museum of Buddhist art spanning Gandhara, Tibet, China and Southeast Asia.

The relic itself rests in a golden stupa on the fourth floor, shown to the public only at set times during chanting ceremonies; check the times posted at the entrance and time your visit around one. Do not miss the roof, where the Ten Thousand Buddha Pagoda holds thousands of small gilt figures and a large Tibetan-style prayer wheel that visitors are invited to turn. Below ground there is a vegetarian dining hall serving complimentary meals, funded by donations — a reminder that a Chinese Buddhist temple is also a charitable institution.

Entry is free, and the temple is open through the daytime, roughly nine to half past six, though the relic chamber follows its own ceremony schedule. Dress modestly, remove shoes where the signs ask, silence your phone and do not use flash. Treat the chanting halls as the working religious spaces they are, and step around anyone who is praying.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry, including the museum floors; the basement vegetarian hall serves complimentary meals and accepts donations. Verify current opening times at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Generally open daily in the daytime, roughly 9:00–18:30, with the relic chamber on the fourth floor viewable only during set chanting ceremonies. Hours can change on festival days — confirm at the entrance.
stops.accessibility: Lifts serve the upper floors and the main hall is step-free, but this is a working temple and the aisles can be tightly crowded. The relic chamber sits on the fourth floor.
stops.insiderTip: Ask at the entrance for the day's relic-viewing ceremony times and build your visit around one — otherwise the fourth floor is just a closed door. Then go up to the roof for the Ten Thousand Buddha Pagoda and the big prayer wheel most visitors miss.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue north up South Bridge Road for about a hundred metres, then turn right into Smith Street. Walk a short block; the Chinatown Complex is the big block on your right, and the hawker centre is up on the second floor.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Chainwit., CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Chinatown Complex Hawker Centre
stops.narration:
Go up to the second floor and you are standing in the biggest hawker centre in Singapore — more than two hundred stalls under one fluorescent roof. A hawker centre is a government-built hall of rented food stalls with shared tables, invented from the 1950s onward to move unlicensed street cooks off the roads and into somewhere with running water. In 2020 UNESCO put Singapore's hawker culture on its intangible-heritage list, calling these halls "community dining rooms", which is exactly what they are: everyone eats here, and everyone eats at the same stalls.

This building is itself a piece of history. It opened in 1983 as the Kreta Ayer Complex, built to house the street hawkers who had cooked along these lanes for generations. The name on the neighbourhood is older still: Kreta Ayer is Malay for "water cart", and the Chinese name for the area, Niu Che Shui, means "bullock-cart water" — because early Chinatown had no piped supply, and water arrived on carts drawn by animals. Smith Street outside was the Cantonese theatre street, home from 1887 to the Lai Chun Yuen opera house, whose crowds once spilled into the food stalls.

Read the hall like a map of migration. Chinatown was settled mainly by Cantonese, Hokkien and Teochew speakers, each with its own food, and you will find all three here alongside Sichuan and northern Chinese cooking from a newer wave of migrants. Find the stall with the longest queue and join it; the famous example in this hall is a soya-sauce chicken rice stall that in 2016 became the first street-food stall anywhere to win a Michelin star — it lost the star again in 2021, which tells you how fast reputations move here.

A few mechanics make the place work. Stalls display hygiene grades from A down to D, inspected and posted on the wall. You order and pay at the stall, cash or a local payment app, then claim a table — a pack of tissues left on a seat is the local way of reserving it. Since 2021 it has been an offence to leave your tray and crockery behind, so return them to the rack when you finish. Most stalls trade from breakfast through the afternoon and many close by early evening, with some resting on Mondays; check what is open before you commit.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter; you pay each stall directly, mostly in cash or by local payment app, with most dishes a few S$ each. Prices and stall opening days change — verify on the day.
stops.openingHours: Hawker stalls generally run from breakfast through the afternoon, with many closing by late evening and some shut on Mondays; individual stalls keep their own hours and rest days. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Lift and escalator up to the second-floor hawker centre, but the aisles are narrow and the tables tightly packed, and it is hard to navigate with a wheelchair at peak times.
stops.insiderTip: Claim a table first by leaving a pack of tissues on it, then queue — that is the local etiquette, not rudeness. And return your tray to the rack when you finish; since 2021 leaving it behind is an offence.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk to Chinatown MRT station, right beside the complex on Pagoda Street. Take the Downtown line north to Little India — about six stops, roughly twelve minutes. The whole way on foot is 3.4 km, about forty-eight minutes in the heat, so ride it. From Little India station, follow the signs to Serangoon Road and walk about two hundred metres north to the temple at number 141.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Kbseah, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple
stops.narration:
You are in the middle of Little India, at its oldest temple. A shrine to the goddess stood here as early as 1855, raised by Tamil labourers who worked the lime kilns nearby — the temple's old Tamil name, Soonambu Kambam Kovil, means "temple at the village of lime". The temple proper was built by Bengali labourers in 1881, and the structure you see is largely a 1986 rebuild on the same conserved site. Look up at the gopuram and read it as a picture book: every figure is a story, and the colours are repainted as part of the temple's upkeep.

The goddess is Kali, here called Veeramakaliamman, the brave Kali — a fierce form of the consort of Shiva, one of the three great gods of Hinduism. Kali is the destroyer of evil and of ignorance, shown in her shrines garlanded with skulls and standing over a demon; her gentler side, Parvati, appears with her sons Ganesha and Murugan. Tamil settlers in a strange colonial city turned to her for protection, for recovery from illness and, the records say, for help conceiving a child. The temple sheltered more than twenty homeless people a night and fed them through the Japanese Occupation of 1942 to 1945.

Little India itself was never planned as a home for Indians. The Raffles plan put the Indian quarter, the Chulia Kampong, on the other side of the river; this area was cattle country, run by European traders with Indian workers rearing and slaughtering the animals, which is why the Malay name for the district, Kandang Kerbau, means "buffalo pens". When the swamps were drained and the cattle trade moved out, the workers stayed, and the neighbourhood became South Asian. It was gazetted as a conservation area in 1989, which is what saved its shophouses.

The district has a harder modern story too. In December 2013 a construction worker named Sakthivel Kumarvelu was killed by a bus at a junction just up the road, and the accident set off a riot — the worst in Singapore in decades — followed by a public-drinking ban across the island at night. Little India runs on migrant labour, most visibly on Sundays, when the workers' one day off fills Serangoon Road with crowds, colour and noise. Treat the men in the crowd as people going about their weekend, not as part of the scenery. Entry is free, shoes come off, and the temple is busiest on Tuesdays, Fridays and Sundays.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry; donations are welcome. It is a working temple, so give generously only if you wish to.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily in morning and evening sessions, roughly 5:30–12:30 and 17:00–21:00, and busiest on Tuesdays, Fridays and Sundays. Confirm at the gate, as festival days shift the times.
stops.accessibility: Level pavement entry, then steps and raised thresholds inside; shoes come off. Not step-free throughout, and very crowded on Sundays and festival days.
stops.insiderTip: Come on a Tuesday, Friday or Sunday to see the temple at full voice, and watch the priests make offerings at the Kali shrine. On Sundays the whole of Serangoon Road outside becomes the event.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the temple and cross to the east side of Serangoon Road, then turn into Kerbau Road just south of the temple. Walk about two hundred metres; the House of Tan Teng Niah is the candy-coloured villa on your left.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: House of Tan Teng Niah
stops.narration:
This small, riotously coloured villa is the last surviving Chinese house in Little India, and it tells you something the guidebooks usually skip: these districts were never as separate as their names suggest. It was built in 1900 by Tan Teng Niah, a towkay — the Hokkien word for a Chinese businessman or boss — who ran a nearby factory and is said to have built the house for his wife. A Chinese merchant, living and working in the heart of the Indian quarter, at the time when the whole point of the town plan had been to keep the communities apart.

Read the building like a lesson in the local vernacular. It has eight rooms and, along the front, a covered arcade: the five-foot way, the continuous sheltered walkway that Raffles ordered every shophouse to provide so that pedestrians could move through the town out of the sun and the monsoon rain. That arcade is now the signature of the shophouse all over Singapore and Malaysia. Look at the doorway too, for the carved pintu pagar — a half-height outer door that swings open to let in air while keeping the interior private — and for the gilded nameplate above the entrance, which reads "Siew Song".

The villa was restored and conserved in the 1980s, and its rainbow paint job has since made it one of the most photographed buildings in the city. It is a private building and not open to the public inside, so enjoy it from the street. Stand back on the opposite pavement for the full facade, then notice where you are standing: this lane is Kerbau Road, and kerbau is Malay for buffalo. You are walking through what was once the cattle yard of the colonial town, a trade worked by Indian labourers and financed by European traders — the economic engine that turned a district of pens and slaughterhouses into one of the most vivid neighbourhoods in Asia.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to view from the street. It is a private building and not open inside.
stops.openingHours: Exterior viewable at all hours; the interior is private and closed to visitors. Admire it from the street.
stops.accessibility: Viewed from the street, where the pavement is level. There are a step or two up into the shophouse arcade, and the interior is not open.
stops.insiderTip: Cross to the far pavement for the whole rainbow facade in one frame, then walk up close to find the carved half-height pintu pagar door and the gilded "Siew Song" nameplate above the entrance that most photographers miss.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the villa, walk south-west about a hundred and fifty metres to Buffalo Road. Tekka Centre sits at the corner of Serangoon Road and Bukit Timah Road, directly on top of Little India MRT station.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Rosanazareth, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Tekka Centre
stops.narration:
This is the beating heart of Little India, and it is three things at once: a wet market, a hawker centre and a block of shops, all wrapped around Little India MRT station. Start with the name, because it is a small lesson in how Singapore talks. The Malay name for the area is Kandang Kerbau, "buffalo pens", from the slaughterhouses that stood here until the 1920s — the same name survives in the Kandang Kerbau women's and children's hospital nearby. In Hokkien the market was called Tek Kia Kha, "foot of the small bamboos", after the bamboo that grew along the canal, and that became Tekka Pasar. The market was first built in 1915, renamed Tekka Centre in 2000, and reopened after a big renovation in 2009.

Walk the ground floor and you get the whole point of the place: Chinese stallholders who speak Tamil, Tamil stallholders who speak Mandarin, and a clientele that does not sort itself by race. Hawker stalls serve South Indian vegetarian meals on banana leaves or steel platters, alongside Chinese vegetarian, North Indian and Malay food. In the wet market you can buy crabs shipped in from Sri Lanka and vegetables flown in from India, next to fish and greens from the region. The flower stalls sell garlands of jasmine, whose scent is the signature smell of this district, and the surrounding shops sell saris, gold, brass oil lamps and cheap tailoring done in minutes.

What you are watching is everyday multiculturalism — not a policy but a habit, built over generations of people sharing a market because they live next door to each other. It is the ground-level version of the ethnic framework you have heard about at every stop: the CMIO model, the public-housing quotas, the careful official management of race. Here it is just commerce and lunch. Come on a Sunday and the whole district outside fills with migrant workers on their one day off; come at lunch on a weekday and you will queue with office workers and construction crews for the same dosa.

Practicals: bring cash or a local payment app, keep small notes, and expect the wet market to wind down by mid-morning while the food stalls run through the day. Individual stalls keep their own rest days, so do not bank on one particular dish — follow whichever queue is longest and you will not go far wrong.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter; you pay each stall or shop directly, mostly in cash or by local payment app. Prices and rest days vary — verify on the day.
stops.openingHours: Hawker stalls roughly 6:30–21:00, the wet market in the morning, and shops through the day. Individual stalls keep their own hours and rest days — confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Level ground floor with lifts and a direct MRT entrance, but the wet-market and hawker aisles are narrow and crowded. Best tackled slowly, and hard in a wheelchair at peak times.
stops.insiderTip: Buy a garland of jasmine at a flower stall — it is the smell of Little India — then find the banana-leaf vegetarian stall and eat with your right hand the way the regulars do. Cutlery is available if you would rather not.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk into Little India MRT station and take the Downtown line two stops to Bugis, about four minutes. On foot it is only about 1.3 km, roughly eighteen minutes straight down Rochor Road, so walking is a real option — take the MRT when the midday sun is at its worst. From Bugis, walk about ten minutes west along North Bridge Road, then turn up Muscat Street; the golden domes are in front of you.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Kari.Shouur, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Sultan Mosque
stops.narration:
Those two golden onion domes belong to the royal mosque of the Sultan of Johor, and they are the reason this district looks the way it does. When the British signed a treaty with Sultan Hussein Shah in 1819 to set up their trading post, they recognised Kampong Glam — kampung means village — as the Sultan's own ground, and a mosque went up beside his palace, completed in 1826 with a contribution of three thousand Spanish dollars from Raffles himself. That first mosque was a low brick building with a two-tiered pitched roof, the classic Southeast Asian style.

By the 1920s it was falling down, so the trustees commissioned a complete rebuild. The architect was an Irishman, Denis Santry of the firm Swan & Maclaren, and between 1925 and 1932 he produced the Indo-Saracenic building in front of you — a European colonial hybrid that mixes Indian and Islamic detail, finished at a cost of two hundred and fifty thousand dollars. Look closely at the base of each dome: it is ringed with the sawn-off ends of glass bottles, collected and donated by poor families who wanted to give something to the mosque. The prayer hall holds five thousand people, and the two minarets are the only ones in Singapore still allowed to broadcast the adhan, the call to prayer, out loud across the rooftops.

Kampong Glam was where the Raffles plan put the Malays, Arabs and Bugis, and it became the Malay-Muslim heart of the colony — and a staging post for the haj, the pilgrimage to Mecca that every able Muslim is expected to make once. Pilgrims gathered here, saved, and sailed. The mosque is still that kind of institution: during Ramadan, the fasting month, the whole neighbourhood turns into a night bazaar, and the start of Ramadan is announced from here.

Visiting rules are strict and worth respecting. Walk-in visitors are welcome Saturday to Thursday, roughly ten to noon and two to four, and the mosque is closed to visitors on Fridays, its busiest prayer day. Entry is free. Use Gate 5, on Bussorah Street, remove your shoes, dress so that arms and legs are covered — robes are lent at the counter — and keep to the permitted areas; the main prayer hall is entered only with an official. Photography without flash is allowed, video is not, and during prayers you stay quiet and out of the way. Hours shift around Ramadan and public holidays, so confirm before you set out.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry for walk-in visitors. Robes are lent free at the counter on a first-come basis. Verify visiting hours before you go, as they change around Ramadan and holidays.
stops.openingHours: Walk-in visitors: Saturday to Thursday 10:00–12:00 and 14:00–16:00; closed to visitors on Fridays. Enter by Gate 5 on Bussorah Street. Confirm before you go — hours change around Ramadan and public holidays.
stops.accessibility: Level entry through Gate 5, with shoes removed on carpeted floors. Some areas, including the main prayer hall, are off-limits to visitors except in the company of a mosque official.
stops.insiderTip: Look at the base of the domes for the ring of glass-bottle ends donated by poor families during the 1930s rebuild — the detail most visitors walk straight past. And come back at dusk to hear the adhan, one of the few broadcast in the country.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the mosque and walk south down Muscat Street, cross North Bridge Road, and continue onto Arab Street. Haji Lane is the narrow lane just off to your right, a two-minute walk.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Chainwit., CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Haji Lane & Arab Street
stops.narration:
This is the narrowest lane on the walk, and its name is a history lesson. Haji Lane takes its name from the Arab pilgrim-brokers who once worked here, arranging the haj — the pilgrimage to Mecca — for Muslims from Singapore and the nearby islands as far away as Java. In the nineteenth century the shophouses along this lane were lodges for pilgrims waiting to sail; while they waited they worked as hawkers to save the rest of their fare. From the 1960s the lane became homes for poorer Malay families, then, as they moved out to new housing estates, it emptied and the shophouses were used for storage.

What saved it was the same conservation wave that saved Chinatown and Little India. From the 1990s the old buildings were restored, and because the rents were low at first, they filled with the tenants no one else wanted: independent boutiques, small cafés, a record shop, a bar or two. That is the story of Haji Lane — a shophouse district saved by gentrification, with all the arguments that go with it. The boutiques and murals are lovely, and they are also a sign of who can afford to be here now. Notice, too, that the two-storey shophouses still wear their five-foot ways and their original proportions; the colour is new, the bones are old.

Turn the corner and Arab Street is a different century of the same story: textile shops, carpet merchants and rattan sellers, families who have traded here for generations, selling the cloth and goods of the Muslim trading world that made Kampong Glam rich. Together the two streets show you both ends of the district's arc — the trade that built it and the tourism that sustains it now.

That is the end of the walk, and you are well placed to stop. Kampong Glam's cafés, bakeries and coffee shops are all around you; order a teh tarik, the pulled milk tea that is the local everyday drink, or a plate of mee goreng, fried noodles, and watch the lane fill up as the light drops. Bugis and Jalan Besar MRT stations are each about ten minutes on foot, and taxis and ride-hail cars pick up along Beach Road. You have crossed three districts that a colonial plan once tried to keep apart, and eaten and walked through the version of the city that grew up in spite of it. Carry that picture home.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk; shops, cafés and restaurants set their own prices.
stops.openingHours: The lane is public at all hours; shops and cafés generally open late morning and stay busy into the evening. Individual businesses keep their own hours.
stops.accessibility: A narrow, level lane with a slightly raised walkway, and a step or two up into the shophouse five-foot ways. Crowded and hard to move through in the evening.
stops.insiderTip: Come in the late afternoon, when the boutiques open and the light hits the murals, then stay for dinner. If you want the district without the crowds, walk one street over to Arab Street for the textile shops and quiet coffee.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Kampong Glam's cafés, bakeries and coffee shops are all around you; Bugis and Jalan Besar MRT stations are each about ten minutes on foot, and taxis and ride-hail cars pick up along Beach Road. Stay for a teh tarik or a plate of mee goreng and watch the lane fill up.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Moheen Reeyad, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
